definition.title: Seasons Simulator
learning_objectives: Explain that axial tilt combined with orbital position changes solar declination during an orbit.
Connect solar declination and observer latitude to noon Sun altitude, incidence angle, geometric day length, and polar day or night.
Compare equal-and-opposite latitudes and explain why their seasonal solar geometry is reversed.
Demonstrate that eccentricity changes Earth-Sun distance and inverse-square flux context but does not create the opposite-hemisphere solar-geometry pattern produced by axial tilt.
Distinguish this conceptual geometry model from a date-specific ephemeris, weather, climate, surface temperature, and observed sunrise or sunset timing.

fields.name: axial_tilt_deg
fields.meaning: Obliquity of the planet in degrees.

fields.name: latitude_deg
fields.meaning: Idealized spherical geographic latitude; north is positive.

fields.name: eccentricity_preset
fields.meaning: Closed set of reviewed distance-context presets.

input_schema.invalid_handling: Reject non-finite values, booleans in numeric fields, out-of-range values, unknown presets, and unsupported serialized state without running the scientific calculation.

definition.default_preset: June-solstice geometry at 40 degrees north with Earth eccentricity.

relationships: Solar declination depends on axial tilt and seasonal orbital position only.
Local-noon solar zenith angle depends on latitude and solar declination.
Noon incidence angle is the local-noon solar zenith angle measured from the outward surface normal.
Geometric day length uses the ideal point-Sun geometric horizon and a 24-hour mean solar day.
Eccentricity is excluded from solar geometry at a fixed orbital position.
Normalized distance uses a fixed Earth-like seasonal perihelion orientation.
Relative solar flux is the inverse square of normalized distance.

equations.noon_zenith: cos(z) = sin(phi) * sin(delta) + cos(phi) * cos(delta); z = acos(clamp(cos(z), -1, 1))
equations.ordinary_day_length: D = 24 * acos(x) / pi hours when -1 < x < 1

calculation_module.valid_domain: Python double-precision arithmetic; finite validated inputs; axial tilt and latitude are bounded in degrees; canonical orbital position is in [0, 360); eccentricity is selected from the reviewed closed preset set.
calculation_module.numerical_policy: Clamp asin and acos arguments only to absorb floating-point roundoff. Fixture tolerances are 1e-9 degree for angles, 1e-9 hour for day length, and 1e-12 relative for dimensionless values; these are arithmetic tolerances, not observational accuracy claims.

output_schema: model version and normalized validated inputs
selected-latitude noon altitude, zenith or incidence angle, day length, and polar state
equal-and-opposite comparison latitude with independently calculated geometry
eccentricity value, normalized Earth-Sun distance, and inverse-square relative solar flux
definition.visualization_module: The browser consumes canonical normalized outputs and applies only disclosed display transforms: normalized orbit coordinates, schematic parallel rays, angle arcs, and textual or bar comparisons. No browser formula reproduces the scientific model.
assumptions: The planet is spherical and the observer is described by idealized geographic latitude.
The Sun's declination is fixed during one mean rotational cycle.
Local solar noon has hour angle zero.
Day length uses the Sun's centre, a geometric horizon, zero atmospheric refraction, no solar-disc radius, and no topographic horizon.
Earth-Sun distance is normalized by the semi-major axis; no absolute kilometre or AU value is manufactured.
The apsidal orientation is fixed to an Earth-like seasonal longitude for deterministic teaching context.
limitations: This is an idealized geometric model, not a date-specific solar ephemeris.
Orbital position is a seasonal angle, not a calendar date, elapsed year fraction, or clock time.
The model does not calculate civil sunrise or sunset, equation of time, weather, climate, surface temperature, or absorbed heating.
Observed sunrise and sunset differ because real observations include atmospheric refraction, solar-disc size, terrain, and other effects.
The exaggerated eccentricity preset is a hypothetical teaching case and is not a claim about Earth or another named planet.
A constant-rate visual phase sweep is not a Kepler elapsed-time propagation and must not be described as days or months.

validation_fixtures.purpose: Independent equinox geometry at equal-and-opposite forty-degree latitudes.
Independent June-solstice hemispheric contrast at forty degrees north and south.
Independent December-solstice swap of the June equal-and-opposite geometry.
Equatorial twelve-hour day and solstitial noon geometry.
Required teaching comparison showing distance context without seasonal solar geometry.
Idealized Arctic-circle boundary classification at both solstices.
Exact point-Sun pole and equinox horizon-all-day degeneracy.
Circular distance context remains exactly normalized at every phase.
Earth preset normalized distance and inverse-square flux at seasonal perihelion.
Earth preset normalized distance and inverse-square flux at the opposite orbital point.
Hypothetical exaggerated preset makes the secondary distance effect visible without changing tilt geometry.

scientific_validation.method: Literal known-case expectations are transcribed from the reviewed Seasons Simulator contract and source-backed constants. Python tests assert those values independently of the production implementation formula; boundary, symmetry, and eccentricity-isolation cases are also exercised.

tools.name: Python pytest
tools.role: Independent contract and boundary assertions using literal scientific reference values.
